item.title: Qiolevu calls for new independent anti-corruption body and stronger discipline among children
item.description: Concerns over possible political influence on corruption investigations and calls for a new independent anti-corruption body have been raised during public consultations on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill in Naitasiri. item.content:encoded:
Concerns over possible political influence on corruption investigations and calls for a new independent anti-corruption body have been raised during public consultations on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill in Naitasiri.

Apenisa Qiolevu, speaking on behalf of the Qaranivalu, the High Chief of Naitasiri, raised these concerns during the Parliamentary Special Committee's second round of public consultations at Navuso Village Hall today.

Qiolevu questions whether FICAC can operate without political influence.

He says political connections and personal relationships could affect corruption investigations, highlighting the need for greater independence and accountability.

Qiolevu proposes establishing a new independent anti-corruption body with support from countries such as Australia, New Zealand and the United States.

He says international assistance could help provide funding, staffing and safeguards to ensure corruption investigations are conducted fairly and independently.

Meanwhile, Qiolevu also raises concerns about children disrespecting their parents and teachers, drug use among young people and the need for stronger discipline.

He says there are growing concerns about how children and young people interpret their constitutional rights, particularly when it comes to respecting parents, teachers and community leaders .

Qiolevu claims some young people are using their rights as an excuse to disregard advice and discipline, while others are becoming involved in drugs and unlawful activities.

He also raises concerns about young people loitering in towns and allegedly causing problems for members of the public.

Qiolevu says some students, young people and members of the public have called for the return of corporal punishment.

He also calls for the English version of the Constitution to use the term "Native Fijians" when referring to Fiji's indigenous people, while retaining "iTaukei ni Vanua o Viti" in the Fijian version.

Qiolevu further suggests replacing the word "changed" with "amended" in Chapter 15 when referring to future amendments to the Constitution.

The consultations will continue at Nakorovatu Village Hall in Vunidawa from 2pm to 4pm and at Muaniweni College Hall in Naitasiri from 6pm to 8pm.

item.title: Lautoka youth leader wants 2013 Constitution to remain in force until after elections
item.description: The proposed amendments to Fiji's 2013 Constitution should be put on hold until after the 2026 general elections, with any changes considered by the incoming government. This has been highlighted by Lautoka youth leader and founder of the One Nation Our People Youth Club, Abdul Zorhab who made the submission during public consultations on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill No. 32 of 2026, telling t
item.content:encoded:
The proposed amendments to Fiji's 2013 Constitution should be put on hold until after the 2026 general elections, with any changes considered by the incoming government.

This has been highlighted by Lautoka youth leader and founder of the One Nation Our People Youth Club, Abdul Zorhab who made the submission during public consultations on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill No. 32 of 2026, telling the parliamentary committee that he does not support amending the current Constitution at this time.

He says while specific clauses may need to be amended, he is not convinced that Fiji needs an entirely new Constitution and believes the process should be reconsidered after the election.

Zorhab questioned the urgency of the proposed amendments, saying families are facing rising living costs, communities are dealing with water shortages, farmers need assistance and young people are leaving Fiji in search of employment opportunities.

He told the committee that his own community had gone without water for three to four days, despite attempts to contact the Water Authority of Fiji and the expectation that water tanks would be delivered.

Zorhab also shared concerns about youth migration, saying his youth club, which was established in 2020 with 45 members, now has only 25, with many of its former members having moved overseas for work.

He says the proposed Bill should also be made available in languages other than English to give people who do not understand English enough time to consider its contents.

Responding to questions from committee members about the consultation and amendment process, Zorhab acknowledged that the process had been underway for almost two years.

However, he pointed to the completion of the Constitution Review Commission's report and draft in August 2026, the introduction of the Government's Bill on 30th September and its progression to the second reading on 2nd October.

He also noted that the parliamentary public consultations began on 15th October, saying the time available for people to understand and respond to the proposed changes was a concern.

Committee member Sachida Nand reminded Zorhab that rising living costs were a global issue and that migration from Fiji had been taking place for many years.

Zorhab maintained that these were among the realities facing communities and questioned why constitutional changes should take priority while people continued to deal with these challenges.

He told the committee that any weaknesses in the current constitution should be clearly identified, independently examined and openly discussed, but says this does not automatically justify replacing the entire Constitution.

item.title: Not declined, but he put a condition that I will not accept - PM
item.description: Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka says National Federation Party Leader, Professor Biman Prasad has not declined his offer to take up the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Employment positions in the coalition cabinet but put a condition that Rabuka will not accept. Speaking to fijivillage News, Rabuka says he withdrew his offer to Professor Prasad and will inform Government House that the swea
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka says National Federation Party Leader, Professor Biman Prasad has not declined his offer to take up the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Employment positions in the coalition cabinet but put a condition that Rabuka will not accept.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Rabuka says he withdrew his offer to Professor Prasad and will inform Government House that the swearing-in ceremony will not take place.

In a letter to the Prime Minister, Professor Prasad has said the prevailing circumstances surrounding the rushed process of the constitution makes his return to Cabinet pointless, and he would be prepared to do so if it was agreed that the constitution amendment process was to be deferred until after the election.

item.title: Namada, Ba resident opens borehole to help families facing water shortages
item.description: As families continue to struggle with water shortages caused by the prolonged dry weather, Tivoro Lane Namada, Ba resident Mohammed Razeel has opened his borehole at home to help those in need. Razeel says water is a basic necessity and nobody should have to struggle when help is available.
item.content:encoded:
As families continue to struggle with water shortages caused by the prolonged dry weather, Tivoro Lane Namada, Ba resident Mohammed Razeel has opened his borehole at home to help those in need.

Razeel says water is a basic necessity and nobody should have to struggle when help is available.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Razeel says his decision to help comes from the heart, as he understands the difficulties families are facing during the current drought.

He says several families and friends have already been collecting water from his home whenever they need it.

Insert: Razeel on assistance MC 17th Nov

Razeel says the shortage is affecting daily household activities including washing, cleaning and maintaining proper hygiene.

He believes helping one another during difficult times is important, as even a small contribution can make a big difference in someone's life.

Razeel is encouraging anyone in need of water to visit his home and collect it.

He says water is life, and supporting one another during difficult times helps build a stronger community.

Those who wish to collect water can contact Razeel on 7308300.

item.description: Creating more opportunities for women, supporting small businesses and improving the lives of rural communities are among the key priorities outlined for Noleen Billings, following her appointment as Deputy Leader of the NextGen Alliance Party. The party says in a statement that Billings brings more than 30 years of experience across business, tourism, education, construction, project management a
item.content:encoded:
Creating more opportunities for women, supporting small businesses and improving the lives of rural communities are among the key priorities outlined for Noleen Billings, following her appointment as Deputy Leader of the NextGen Alliance Party.

The party says in a statement that Billings brings more than 30 years of experience across business, tourism, education, construction, project management and community development.

Her professional background includes project consultancy, business management and supporting women and local businesses in rural communities.

The party says Billings will focus on expanding economic opportunities, strengthening rural development and promoting sustainable growth.

The appointment also reflects the party's commitment to bringing people with diverse professional backgrounds and community experience into leadership roles.

The NextGen Alliance Party says it aims to encourage greater community participation and build a stronger, more self-reliant Fiji.

item.title: Fiji cannot tackle growing challenges alone - Rabuka
item.description: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has called on Fiji’s development partners to work more closely with the Government as the country faces growing challenges, including the cost of living, drug-related harm, rising HIV cases and the effects of climate change. Speaking at a joint high-level Government and development partners meeting at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, Rabuka says these challenges are
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has called on Fiji’s development partners to work more closely with the Government as the country faces growing challenges, including the cost of living, drug-related harm, rising HIV cases and the effects of climate change.

Speaking at a joint high-level Government and development partners meeting at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, Rabuka says these challenges are placing increasing pressure on families, communities and essential public services.

He says many Fijian families continue to struggle with the cost of living, while uncertainty in global fuel supply and prices is also affecting businesses and the Government’s ability to deliver services.

Rabuka says the growing drug problem is another major concern, with its effects reaching beyond law enforcement and affecting public health, family life and the future of young people.

He says the drug crisis is closely linked to Fiji’s growing HIV emergency, with unsafe drug injecting identified as a major cause of transmission.

Rabuka says almost half of the people who started HIV treatment in 2024 were people who inject drugs.

He says the Government is committed to stopping the supply and distribution of illegal drugs, but enforcement alone will not solve the problem.

He says more attention must also be given to prevention, rehabilitation, community support, testing and treatment.

Rabuka is also calling for more accessible and reliable climate financing, saying Fiji and other Pacific countries are facing some of the worst effects of climate change despite contributing the least to the problem.

He says climate change is threatening communities, infrastructure, food supplies and water security.

The Prime Minister says ageing hospitals, roads, bridges, ports and water systems are also putting pressure on the country’s development.

He says the Government cannot address these challenges alone and needs stronger partnerships, technical expertise and financial support.

Rabuka says development assistance must be directed towards Fiji’s national pri orities and deliver real benefits to the people.

During the meeting, development partners will also be presented with several major projects requiring support, including the redevelopment of the Colonial War Memorial Hospital, flood alleviation projects and the proposed Rokopili Transhipment Port.

Rabuka says these projects are important investments that will improve healthcare, protect communities from flooding and strengthen economic opportunities.

He also highlighted the proposed constitutional changes, saying Parliament is expected to consider the third reading of the Constitution Amendment Bill during its sitting from November 30th to December 4th.

He says if the Bill is passed, the country will proceed to a national referendum, while if it is not passed, Fiji will move towards a general election.

Rabuka says the Government remains committed to a free, fair, peaceful and credible democratic process.

He has urged development partners to engage openly with the Government, to identify gaps in existing support and work together on practical solutions that will improve the lives of Fijians.
